title: Re-handling an axe, hammer, maul or file
summary: Fit a new wooden handle to an axe, hammer, maul or sledge head, or a file, from straight-grained hickory, ash or oak. A poor fit or wrong grain lets the head work loose and fly off; a dry handle, a full-depth wooden wedge and a pin keep it on.

materials.item: Handle or handle blank: straight-grained hickory, ash or oak, dry, with no knots
Wooden wedge, dry hardwood or softwood, as long as the eye front to back
Sandpaper, about 100 grit, or a scraper
Steel roll pin, 5/32 or 3/16 in (about 4 or 5 mm)
Steel or round ring wedge, if the maker's head was hung with one

steps.text: Put on safety glasses or goggles and gloves before you start: you will be hammering a drift and wedges (Warwood handle, CCOHS struck). Clamp the old handle in a vise and saw it off just below the head (Ax Manual ch9).

Hold the head in a wooden jig, drill a few holes down into the stub to loosen it, keeping clear of any steel wedges, then drive it out with a drift and hammer, from the narrow bottom of the eye toward the wider top (Ax Manual ch9).
steps.warn: Don't hammer on the head itself to shift a handle, and don't crush an axe eye in a tight vise (Ax Manual ch9, ch10).

steps.text: Clean the eye out. Leave the new handle overnight in a warm, dry room so it has finished drying before the final fit (Council care); wood that shrinks after hanging leaves the head loose (Gränsfors care).

Check the new wood: straight grain the full length, no knots or runout, and end grain whose growth-ring lines run the same way as the head, front to back, parallel to the wedge slot (AATG hanging, Ax Manual ch6, Trail handles).

Try the handle in the bottom of the eye. Rasp only the part that goes into the eye, a little at a time, until it goes in with light force; at this stage a slightly loose fit is fine (Ax Manual ch10, AATG hanging).
steps.warn: Rasping can't be undone. Take too much and the head sits loose for good (AATG hanging, Trail handles).

steps.text: Seat the head by standing it on a solid surface with the handle upright and striking the end (heel) of the handle with a wooden or rubber mallet; use enough force to make it move, not so much that you can't get it off again (Ax Manual ch10 and its figure 10-9, Warwood handle).
Sight down an axe's cutting edge to the knob of the handle; take wood off one side of the eye section to straighten it (Ax Manual ch10).
Make the slot (kerf) in the top of the handle deep enough for the wedge to reach one-half to three-quarters of the way down the eye; deepen it with a handsaw if needed (Ax Manual ch10, AATG hanging).
Drive the head fully home with the mallet, then drive the wooden wedge into the slot until it stops. No linseed oil on the wedge or in the eye (Ax Manual ch9, ch10, Council care).
Saw off the waste wedge and handle top. Leave about 6 to 12 mm (1/4 to 1/2 in) of handle above the head (Ax Manual ch10).

If you use a steel wedge, drive it straight and evenly (Warwood handle). The Forest Service says that if you must use steel crosstie wedges in the field, put one along each side of the wooden wedge in the same slot, not across it (Ax Manual ch10).
steps.warn: Steel wedges crush wood fibres and can split the handle; the Forest Service uses wooden wedges only (Ax Manual ch10, AATG hanging).

steps.text: For a work axe, drill through head and handle about one-fifth of the way up from the bottom of the head, below the wedge, and drive in a roll pin (Ax Manual ch10).
Rub linseed oil into the handle, several thin coats, wiping off the excess (Ax Manual ch9, ch10).
steps.warn: Oily rags can catch fire on their own: dry them spread out outdoors or keep them in water (Ax Manual ch9, AATG hanging). Wear gloves with old stock boiled linseed oil, which may contain lead (Ax Manual ch9).

steps.text: Give it a few test swings into wood, look for any gap between head and handle, and check it again after the first day's work (Warwood handle, Gränsfors care).

notes:
## When a handle is worth replacing
A cracked, split or splintered handle comes off; so does one so shrunken that re-wedging won't tighten it (CCOHS hammers, Ax Manual ch12). A loose head on a sound handle often needs only a new wedge (AATG hanging). Check the head first with [Checking a found hammer, axe, maul or sledge](#guides/test_striking_tools): no point hanging a cracked head. This guide is written round the axe, which the Forest Service covers in detail; hammers, mauls and sledges hang the same way, with a wooden wedge in a slot and the handle driven tight (Council care, Warwood handle).

## Wood for a handle
| Wood | Use it for | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Hickory | The first choice for striking-tool handles | Purdue FNR-270, Ax Manual ch6 |
| White ash | Long tool handles; also suitable for axes | Purdue FNR-270, Ax Manual ch6 |
| Oak | Suitable for axe handles | Ax Manual ch6 |
| Hard (sugar) maple | Purdue lists it for furniture and athletic equipment, not tool handles, and no handle source here names it: use it only if there is no hickory, ash or oak, and check the grain closely | Purdue FNR-270 |
| Soft (red, silver) maple | Not where strength matters | Purdue FNR-270 |
| Pine, fir, spruce | No | Ax Manual ch6 |

Purdue gives densities of about 51 lb/ft³ (820 kg/m³) for shagbark hickory, 44 (700) for sugar maple and 39 (620) for white ash (Purdue FNR-270). The Forest Service says not to overlook other woods, especially for a light axe or hatchet; other countries use beech and other less dense woods (Ax Manual ch6). To tell a softwood, press your thumbnail into the side: if it dents easily, it's probably softwood (Ax Manual ch6).

Where to find it after a disaster:
- **Broken long handles.** Long tool handles are a main use of ash (Purdue FNR-270, MN DNR ash), so a snapped shovel or rake handle may be good ash; check the grain as below. A broken axe handle still has enough good wood for a rasp or file handle (Ax Manual ch7).
- **Wooden baseball bats.** Ash is a bat wood (Purdue FNR-270, MN DNR ash); check the grain as for any blank. Aluminium and composite bats are no use.
- **Furniture.** Hickory, ash and sugar maple all go into furniture (Purdue FNR-270): look at thick chair and table legs and bed rails. Old paint may contain lead: wet it and scrape it outdoors, never sand it ([lead](#browse/hazards/lead)).
- Red and white hickory (heartwood and sapwood) are equally strong, so colour doesn't matter (Ax Manual ch6).

## Grain: the part that matters most
- **Straight, full length.** The grain should run the length of the handle with no knots. Where it runs out the side, front or back ("runout"), the handle splits there (Ax Manual ch6, AATG hanging).
- **Rings in line with the head.** Look at the end grain at the top of the handle. The growth-ring lines should run the same way as the head, front to back, parallel to the slot for the wedge. Grain running across the head is more likely to break (AATG hanging, Ax Manual ch6, Trail handles).
- **Ring count** is argued about (some want no more than 17 rings per inch); the Forest Service author rates species and grain direction above it (Ax Manual ch6).
- **No paint or varnish** on a handle you are choosing: it hides flaws, and an oil finish is better for your hands (Trail handles, Ax Manual ch9).

## Shaping a new handle
A thinner handle is stronger in use than a thick one: it flexes, hits harder and sends less shock to your hands and the eye joint (Ax Manual ch9). Shape it with a rasp, spokeshave, drawknife or a scraper blade, with the handle held in a vise (Ax Manual ch9). Take wood off the sides and back, not the belly, and keep it oval or eight-sided rather than round so it doesn't turn in your hands (Ax Manual ch9). For a full-size axe, handles run 81 to 91 cm (32 to 36 in) for heads of 1.4 to 2.7 kg (3 to 6 lb) (AATG hanging). Sand smooth, leaving the grip a little rough (Ax Manual ch9). The Forest Service publishes drawings of a handle jig and drift pins (Ax Manual appB).

## Wedges, glue and pins
- **Wooden wedge, full depth.** The wedge spreads the top of the handle against the walls of the eye. It should run the full length of the eye front to back and reach one-half to three-quarters of the way down (Ax Manual ch10). The Forest Service uses dry hardwood such as yellow poplar (AATG hanging) or prefers softwood, which swells and shrinks with the handle (Ax Manual ch10). If the head works loose later, drive the wedge further or fit a thicker one (Ax Manual ch12).
- **Steel wedges.** The Forest Service avoids them: they crush the handle wood, don't move with the weather, and can split the handle (AATG hanging, Ax Manual ch10, Trail handles). Many store-bought axes come with a small steel crosstie wedge (Ax Manual ch10); Council Tool says to replace steel wedges as needed, and Warwood offers one as an option over the wooden wedge (Council care, Warwood handle). If you must add one in the field, the Forest Service says to drive one along each side of the wooden wedge in the same slot, not across it, and that round metal ferrules spread the force best (Ax Manual ch10). Warwood says to centre a round or flat steel wedge on the top of the handle and tap it in straight and evenly so the wood doesn't split (Warwood handle).
- **Glue and epoxy.** The Forest Service isn't of one mind: An Ax to Grind says not to use epoxy (AATG hanging), but Handtools for Trail Work fills voids round the wedge with epoxy and soaks epoxy-bonded heads in boiling water to get them off (Trail handles). Warwood allows glue on the wooden wedge as an option (Warwood handle), and Gränsfors notes that heads fixed with a wedge or glue can both come loose if the handle wasn't properly dried (Gränsfors care).
- **Water.** The Forest Service discourages soaking a handle to swell it: the crushed fibres don't recover and the head ends up looser once it dries (Ax Manual ch12). An Ax to Grind and Handtools for Trail Work allow it only as a short-term emergency field fix, with a proper repair as soon as possible (AATG hanging, Trail handles). A pin stops a loosened head flying off (Ax Manual ch10, ch12).
- **Pin.** A roll pin through head and handle, low in the eye and below the wedge, stops a loose head flying off; the Forest Service pins its work axes (Ax Manual ch10).

## Linseed oil
Rub raw or boiled linseed oil into the finished handle in several thin coats; boiled dries faster (Ax Manual ch9, ch10). Keep it off the part inside the eye and off the wedge, where it acts as a lubricant (Ax Manual ch9, ch10). Re-oil often at first: once a day for a week, once a week for a month, once a month for a year, then once a year (Ax Manual ch9). Old stock boiled linseed oil may contain lead driers: wear latex or nitrile gloves (Ax Manual ch9). Oil-soaked rags can heat up and catch fire: dry them spread out outdoors, or keep them under water ([self-heating](#browse/hazards/self_heating), Ax Manual ch9).

## File and rasp handles
Never use a file without a tight handle: if the file slips, a bare tang goes into your palm (Ax Manual ch7). The Forest Service author made a rasp handle from a broken axe handle (Ax Manual ch7).
- **Drilled fit.** Woodcraft's method for tanged chisels: drill a hole a little smaller than the tang and a little deeper than it is long, stepped for a tapered tang, then drive the handle on (Woodcraft handles).
- **Burning in.** Woodcraft's second method: drill a 3 mm (1/8 in) pilot hole the length of the tang, clamp the tool tang-up, heat until about 2 cm (3/4 in) of the tip glows deep red, push the handle onto it until about 3 mm (1/8 in) short of the shoulder, cool the tang, then tap the handle home. Only the tip is heated, which burns the wood without taking the temper out of the tool (Woodcraft handles). Woodcraft's sheet is written for tanged chisels and gouges. No source here gives a burn-in method for a file (Ax Manual ch8 is about ax heads, not files), so for a file use the drilled fit above and don't heat it. The glowing tang burns skin ([hot surfaces](#browse/hazards/burn)).

Once the head is on, see [Axe and hatchet care](#guides/skill_axe_care) for sharpening and use.
